title: Congenital Pulmonary Diseases
subject: Respiratory System (RESP)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers lung and airway disease present from birth: one single-gene disorder, cystic fibrosis, and four errors of foregut and diaphragm development (tracheoesophageal fistula, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, pulmonary sequestration, and bronchogenic cyst). Board questions describe a newborn who chokes with feeds, a baby in distress with a sunken abdomen, a child with salty skin and greasy stools, or a teenager with repeated pneumonia in one lower lobe, and ask you to name the lesion and explain its findings. The unifying skill is tracing every sign back to one transport defect or one wrong turn in embryology.

connections.to: Gastrointestinal system (exocrine pancreas and small bowel)
connections.how: The same CFTR defect that dehydrates airway mucus plugs pancreatic ducts and thickens meconium, causing steatorrhea and meconium ileus.
Staphylococcus aureus and mucoid Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilms exploit retained CF mucus, and infected sequestrations and cysts show why drainage matters more than the organism.
Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens explains male infertility in CF with normal sperm production in the testes.
Pulmonary hypoplasia in diaphragmatic hernia causes persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn, and cardiac defects are a core part of the VACTERL association.
The sweat duct is the clearest tissue in which to see CFTR absorbing rather than secreting chloride, which is the basis of the sweat test.

sections.title: Cystic fibrosis: the clinical picture across organs and ages

blocks.text: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive loss of CFTR function, most often from the F508del variant, which misfolds and is degraded before reaching the cell surface (PU-10). Every organ problem follows one rule: an epithelium that should secrete chloride, bicarbonate, and water cannot, so its secretions become thick, acidic, and protein rich, and they block the lumen they drain into. The problems appear in a predictable order with age.
Newborn and infant

Meconium ileus is often the first sign. Dehydrated, sticky meconium plugs the distal ileum, causing abdominal distension, bilious vomiting, and failure to pass meconium in the first days. It occurs in about 15 to 20% of affected newborns, and most infants with meconium ileus (about 80 to 90%) have CF. The pancreas is damaged before birth: without fluid and bicarbonate to flush them, ducts fill with inspissated enzyme secretions, acini are destroyed, and the gland is replaced by fibrosis and fat. About 85% of patients have exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, so fat and protein are poorly digested. The result is steatorrhea (bulky, greasy, foul stools), failure to thrive despite a good appetite, and deficiency of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K. Infants who lose salt in sweat during hot weather can develop hyponatremic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.
Lungs and sinuses

The airways are normal at birth. Dehydrated mucus is not cleared, bacteria persist, and neutrophils flood in; their elastase and released DNA thicken the mucus further and digest the bronchial wall. Early colonizers are Staphylococcus aureus and Haemophilus influenzae. Pseudomonas aeruginosa follows and converts to a mucoid form that secretes alginate, a polysaccharide that builds a biofilm resistant to phagocytes and antibiotics. The repeated cycle of obstruction, infection, and inflammation produces bronchiectasis, permanent dilation of bronchi, predominantly in the upper lobes, with chronic productive cough, digital clubbing, hemoptysis, and eventually hypoxemia, cor pulmonale, and respiratory failure, the usual cause of death. In the upper airway the same dehydration causes chronic sinusitis and nasal polyps; polyps in a child are unusual enough that CF should be considered.

blocks.text: Reproduction and diagnosis

About 95% of men with CF are infertile from congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens: the duct is thought to be obstructed by thick secretions in fetal life and then to degenerate, so the testes make sperm normally but cannot deliver them (obstructive azoospermia with low ejaculate volume). Some men with milder CFTR variants have only this finding.

Most cases are now suspected from a raised immunoreactive trypsinogen on newborn screening, a marker of pancreatic duct injury, or from the clinical picture above. Diagnosis requires evidence of CFTR dysfunction, classically a sweat chloride of 60 mmol/L or higher on a properly collected pilocarpine-stimulated sample. Values of 30 to 59 mmol/L are intermediate and need CFTR genotyping, and values below 30 mmol/L make CF unlikely. In a child with a positive screen or typical features, two disease-causing CFTR variants also establish it.

sections.title: Why sweat is salty while the airway surface dries out

blocks.text: CFTR is a passive channel: chloride moves through it down its electrochemical gradient, so the tissue, not the channel, sets the direction. Airway cells load chloride above equilibrium and release it into the lumen; the sweat duct takes chloride from a salty lumen into the cell. Losing the channel stops secretion in one tissue and absorption in the other.
The sweat duct: failed absorption

An eccrine sweat gland has two parts. The secretory coil produces a primary fluid that is nearly isotonic with plasma, with sodium and chloride about 140 and 105 mmol/L. As this fluid flows up the duct, the duct cells reabsorb sodium through apical ENaC and chloride through apical CFTR, and the Na+/K+-ATPase on the basolateral side moves sodium on into the interstitium. The duct is nearly impermeable to water, so salt is recovered while water stays behind, and normal sweat reaching the skin is hypotonic, with chloride usually below 30 mmol/L.

Without CFTR, the duct has almost no route for chloride to leave the lumen. Sodium cannot be absorbed alone for long: as positive charge leaves, the lumen becomes strongly negative and opposes further sodium entry, so sodium absorption falls too. Both ions stay in the sweat, and sweat chloride rises toward the primary-fluid value, usually above 60 mmol/L. Hence salty-tasting skin and salt depletion in hot weather. Secretion by the coil is largely intact because cholinergic sweating can use other chloride channels, so the volume of sweat is roughly normal.

blocks.text: The airway: failed secretion with excess sodium absorption

Chloride enters the cell across the basolateral membrane through the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC1), accumulates above equilibrium, and exits through apical CFTR; sodium follows paracellularly and water follows osmotically, adding liquid. At the same time ENaC absorbs sodium, chloride follows, and water is drawn out. CFTR normally restrains ENaC, so the two processes balance and keep the periciliary layer about 7 micrometers deep, the height of an extended cilium.

In CF the secretory arm is lost, and in the classic model ENaC is released from restraint, so sodium absorption increases. Salt and water are pulled out of the lumen, the periciliary layer collapses, and mucus presses onto the cilia, which can no longer beat it forward. Lost bicarbonate secretion also acidifies the liquid, impairing mucin expansion and antimicrobial peptides. Unlike sweat, airway liquid in CF is not saltier: there is simply less of it. The more negative nasal potential difference in CF reflects the increased sodium absorption.

blocks.title: One channel, opposite jobs
rows: Too little surface liquid; thick mucus
blocks.caption: The chloride gradient in each tissue decides whether CFTR loss blocks absorption or secretion.

blocks.predict: If CFTR loss reduces chloride movement in both tissues, why does the sweat test show too much chloride while the airway shows too little liquid?
blocks.explain: The water-tight sweat duct normally removes salt from a fixed volume, so failure leaves the concentration high. The airway normally adds chloride and water, so failure, plus unchecked ENaC absorption, lowers liquid volume while composition changes little.

blocks.text: In week 4 the respiratory diverticulum (lung bud) grows from the ventral wall of the foregut. Tracheoesophageal ridges then grow in from each side and fuse into the tracheoesophageal septum, dividing the foregut into the trachea in front and the esophagus behind (PU-1). If the septum deviates posteriorly or the ridges fail to fuse, the esophagus loses its continuity and an opening between airway and gut persists. Atresia and fistula therefore usually occur together, in about 1 in 3,000 to 4,500 births.
The most common form, about 85% of cases, is esophageal atresia with a distal fistula: the upper esophagus ends in a blind pouch, and the lower esophagus opens into the trachea near the carina.

blocks.caption: The blind pouch explains the feeding signs; the distal fistula explains gastric air and chemical pneumonitis.

blocks.text: Polyhydramnios develops because the fetus normally swallows amniotic fluid and absorbs it in the intestine, while fetal urine keeps adding fluid. After birth, saliva and the first feed fill the small upper pouch and spill into the larynx. Cyanosis comes from aspiration and laryngospasm, and from a stomach distended by air pumped through the fistula with each cry, which pushes up the diaphragm. The bedside clue is a nasogastric tube that stops at about 10 cm; a radiograph shows it coiled in the upper pouch, and gas in the stomach and bowel proves that a distal fistula connects the airway to the gut. Acid gastric content refluxing up the fistula causes chemical pneumonitis.

Immediate aspiration of feeds from the upper segment
blocks.caption: Frequencies vary between series; the distal fistula type is consistently the most common.

blocks.text: About half of affected infants have another anomaly, so finding one should start a search. The VACTERL association groups vertebral defects, anal atresia, cardiac defects (often ventricular septal defect), tracheoesophageal fistula, esophageal atresia, renal anomalies, and limb defects, typically of the radial ray. It is an association, not a syndrome with a single cause, and is usually diagnosed when at least three components are present. Many infants also have tracheomalacia, a soft trachea at the fistula site that collapses on expiration.

blocks.title: Reading the newborn radiograph
blocks.text: A newborn of a pregnancy complicated by polyhydramnios drools and coughs with the first feed. A tube stops at 10 cm. Step 1: the tube cannot reach the stomach, so the esophagus is interrupted; the radiograph shows it coiled in the upper chest. Step 2: look below the diaphragm. A gas-filled stomach means air reached it, and the only route left is a fistula from the trachea to the lower esophagus, the common type. Step 3: if the abdomen were gasless, the lower segment has no connection to the airway, pointing to isolated atresia, which also explains the more severe polyhydramnios. Step 4: examine the spine, anus, heart, kidneys, and radii for VACTERL.

The diaphragm is assembled from four sources: the septum transversum (central tendon), the two pleuroperitoneal membranes, the dorsal mesentery of the esophagus (crura), and muscle from the body wall at the periphery. The pleuroperitoneal membranes grow from the posterolateral body wall and close the pleuroperitoneal canals, the last openings between the thoracic and abdominal cavities, around week 7. The left canal is larger and closes later than the right.

Congenital diaphragmatic hernia occurs in about 1 in 2,000 to 4,000 births. In most cases a pleuroperitoneal membrane fails to close its canal, leaving a posterolateral (Bochdalek) defect; about 85% are on the left, because the left canal closes later and the liver protects the right side. The timing explains the damage. The midgut lies in the umbilical cord (physiological herniation) until about week 10, and when it returns to the abdomen it can pass through the open canal into the chest. This happens during the pseudoglandular stage, when the bronchial tree is branching.

blocks.title: From an open canal to pulmonary hypoplasia
steps: Pleuroperitoneal membrane fails to close the canal
Returning midgut enters the left hemithorax
Left lung compressed; mediastinum shifts right
Fewer airway branches, alveoli, and arteries in both lungs
Muscular small arteries keep pulmonary resistance high
Hypoxemia and right-to-left shunting after birth
blocks.caption: The lethal problem is the small lung and its vascular bed, not the hernia itself.

blocks.text: Compression during branching leaves both lungs hypoplastic, the ipsilateral lung most. The pulmonary arteries are few in number and muscularized abnormally far into the periphery, so pulmonary vascular resistance fails to fall at birth. Blood then shunts right to left through the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale, producing persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn and profound hypoxemia, often with higher saturation in the right hand than the feet (PU-1).

At birth the infant has severe respiratory distress and cyanosis. The abdomen is scaphoid (sunken) because its contents are in the chest, the chest may look barrel shaped, breath sounds are absent on the left, bowel sounds may be heard in the chest, and heart sounds are displaced to the right by mediastinal shift. A radiograph shows gas-filled bowel loops in the left hemithorax and the mediastinum pushed right. Prenatal ultrasound often detects the lesion first.

blocks.caption: Board questions about a newborn in distress with a sunken abdomen are almost always describing the Bochdalek type.

blocks.predict: Why does an infant with a left-sided hernia often have hypoplasia of the right lung as well?
blocks.explain: Herniated bowel pushes the mediastinum toward the right, compressing the right lung during the same branching period, so both lungs develop fewer airways and arteries.

blocks.text: Both lesions arise from abnormal budding of the foregut, and both tend to become infected, but they differ in what they connect to. The two questions to ask of any congenital lung mass are where its blood comes from and whether it drains into an airway.
Pulmonary sequestration

A sequestration is a mass of lung tissue that does not communicate with the normal tracheobronchial tree and receives its arterial blood from a systemic artery, usually from the descending thoracic or upper abdominal aorta, instead of from the pulmonary artery. It is thought to come from an accessory lung bud arising from the foregut below the normal one. Because it takes no part in ventilation, it performs no gas exchange. It most often lies in a lower lobe, usually the left posterior basal segment. Two forms are recognized. An intralobar sequestration lies within the visceral pleura of a normal lobe and usually drains to the pulmonary veins; it is the more common form and often presents in later childhood or adulthood. An extralobar sequestration has its own pleural covering, usually drains to systemic veins such as the azygos system, presents in infancy, and is more often associated with other anomalies, including diaphragmatic hernia.

Without a bronchus, secretions cannot be cleared. Bacteria reach the tissue through collateral channels or small acquired airway connections, and the stagnant tissue becomes infected again and again, so the classic presentation is recurrent pneumonia in the same lower lobe segment. Imaging that shows an artery running from the aorta into the mass establishes the diagnosis. A large systemic supply can rarely divert enough aortic flow to cause high-output heart failure.
Bronchogenic cyst

A bronchogenic cyst forms when a small bud separates abnormally from the developing trachea or bronchial tree and grows into a closed sac. Its wall resembles a bronchus, with ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium, cartilage plates, smooth muscle, and seromucous glands, and it fills with mucus or clear fluid. Most lie in the middle mediastinum near the carina or beside the trachea, and fewer lie within the lung. Its blood supply is normal. Many are found incidentally as a round mediastinal mass; others compress the trachea, a bronchus, or the esophagus, causing wheeze, stridor, cough, or dysphagia, or they become infected, especially if they gain a connection to an airway, which then shows an air-fluid level.

rows: Accessory lung bud from the foregut
Abnormal budding of the trachea or bronchial tree

blocks.caption: A systemic artery from the aorta is the single most specific finding for sequestration.

blocks.title: Recurrent pneumonia in one place
blocks.text: A 14-year-old has had three pneumonias, each in the left lower lobe, with full clearing between them. Step 1: recurrence in one site points to a local lesion, not an immune defect, which would cause infections in varied sites and organs. Step 2: a lower lobe posterior basal location suggests sequestration. Step 3: CT angiography shows an artery from the descending aorta entering the mass, confirming systemic supply. Step 4: the tissue lies within the normal pleura and drains to pulmonary veins, so it is intralobar, which fits presentation in adolescence. A bronchogenic cyst would instead appear as a round, fluid-density mass near the carina with normal vessels.

integration.text: Anatomy, embryology, and physiology explain each lesion. The foregut gives rise to the trachea, lungs, and esophagus, so errors in septation produce tracheoesophageal fistula, and abnormal buds produce sequestration and bronchogenic cyst. Lung growth needs stretch and space during the pseudoglandular stage, so a diaphragmatic defect present then leaves hypoplastic lungs and a high-resistance pulmonary circulation. Cystic fibrosis is a transport disease: whether CFTR normally secretes or absorbs chloride in a tissue predicts whether its loss dries secretions (airway, pancreas, intestine, vas deferens) or leaves salt in a fluid (sweat).

Microbiology and pathology tie the conditions together through impaired drainage. Mucus that cannot be cleared from CF airways, aspirated feeds in tracheoesophageal fistula, and secretions trapped in a sequestration all lead to recurrent infection, and the organism matters less than the obstruction. CF severity varies with genotype and environment, so not every patient shows every finding.

summary: Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive CFTR loss; thick, dehydrated secretions block the intestine, pancreas, bile ducts, airways, sinuses, and vas deferens.
Meconium ileus, steatorrhea with A, D, E, K deficiency, S. aureus then mucoid P. aeruginosa, bronchiectasis, nasal polyps, and absent vas deferens form the CF picture.
Sweat chloride of 60 mmol/L or higher supports CF; 30 to 59 is intermediate and below 30 makes CF unlikely.
In the sweat duct CFTR absorbs chloride from a water-tight lumen, so its loss leaves salty sweat.
In the airway CFTR secretes chloride and restrains ENaC, so its loss reduces secretion, increases sodium absorption, and collapses the periciliary layer.
The common tracheoesophageal fistula is a blind upper pouch with a distal fistula: polyhydramnios, drooling, choking and cyanosis with feeds, a coiled tube, and gastric air.
A gasless abdomen means atresia without a distal fistula; an H-type fistula presents late with recurrent aspiration.
VACTERL groups vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, esophageal, renal, and limb anomalies; one should prompt a search for the others.
Bochdalek hernia is a left posterolateral pleuroperitoneal defect; returning bowel compresses the branching lung, causing hypoplasia, pulmonary hypertension, and a scaphoid abdomen.
Sequestration has a systemic arterial supply from the aorta and no bronchial connection; a bronchogenic cyst is a closed, fluid-filled foregut bud near the carina.

verify: The model in which CFTR loss releases ENaC from inhibition and increases airway sodium absorption is the classic teaching named in the objective, but some human and animal studies emphasize reduced chloride and bicarbonate secretion over ENaC hyperabsorption; confirm the emphasis NABNE expects.
Sweat chloride cutoffs (60 mmol/L or higher diagnostic, 30 to 59 intermediate, below 30 unlikely) follow the 2017 CF Foundation consensus; confirm the values NABNE uses.
Percentages for meconium ileus (about 15 to 20%), pancreatic insufficiency (about 85%), and male infertility (about 95%) in CF vary among sources.
Frequencies of esophageal atresia and fistula types (about 85%, 8%, 4%) and of associated anomalies (about half) vary between series.
Timing of pleuroperitoneal canal closure is given as week 6 in some texts and week 7 in others; incidence of diaphragmatic hernia is quoted from 1 in 2,000 to 1 in 5,000.
Whether intralobar sequestration is always congenital or sometimes acquired after chronic infection is debated; the distribution of intralobar versus extralobar forms varies among series.
Primary sweat sodium and chloride concentrations (about 140 and 105 mmol/L) are approximate; the share of meconium ileus cases due to CF (about 80 to 90%) varies among series.
Requested new diagram names for a future revision: cftr-sweat-airway (side by side ion transport in sweat duct and airway cells) and tef-types (the four esophageal atresia and fistula variants).
